items: Concentrated dependency justifies expensive substitution; diversified dependency mostly doesn't. Singapore's water came through pipes from one neighbour whose prime minister had said out loud he could shut them. Its food came from 140 countries, now 187.
Self-sufficiency on unsuitable ground is brutally slow: after years of investment and effort, Brunei moved from 4.8 to 8 per cent of the rice it consumes.

Rankings move without reality moving. Singapore fell from 1st of 113 on the Economist Intelligence Unit's food security index in 2019 to 28th in 2022 mainly because the index started weighting farmer-focused measures and the link between farmers and their nearest market.

Vertical farms and cultured meat aren't blocked by science but by unit economics — high energy costs, hard scaling, and consumers who simply don't care. Singapore was the world's cultured-meat capital in 2022 and watched startups close by 2024.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Resilience is a purchase, not a virtue. Ask what it costs you every year, and whether the risk it buys down is the one you actually face.

recall.q: Singapore solved water self-sufficiency but struggled with food. What made the two problems fundamentally different?
recall.a: Water was a concentrated dependency — roughly half the supply arriving through pipes from a single neighbour whose prime minister had floated shutting them off — so expensive substitution was worth building. Food arrived from a wide spread of suppliers, now 187 countries and regions, into a country already ranked the world's most food-secure, so forcing 30 per cent of consumption onto an island with no comparative advantage in farming meant paying steep opportunity costs against a risk that was

cards.title: Dieting taxes women's attention, not their intelligence
cards.body: Ancel Keys starved 36 men in 1944 and their measured intelligence came through it intact; what the hunger took was their attention. An OB-GYN argues that the lifelong management of appetite most women are trained into is not a beauty problem or a discipline problem but a cognitive one — and that the incentives paying for it have been measured too.

sections.text:
The summer before sixth grade, a girl lay on the concrete beside a swimming pool and realised she had not heard most of her teammate's story. She had decided to eat as little as possible before middle school started — a sleeve of fat-free SnackWell's cookies a day, a product engineered to taste like cardboard and sold to women already told that fat was the enemy and appetite was something to be managed rather than answered.

By the end of the week her swimsuit hung loose at the shoulders. On the first day back at school, a friend's mother looked her over the way you assess a renovation that has come out well and said she had a "new figure." She said it warmly, the way adults hand children gifts.

Sarah Berg, the girl in that scene and now an OB-GYN, wants an honest accounting of what was traded there. Something had been taken — the half-heard week, the thoughts that dissolved mid-sentence into how long until dinner — and something had been handed back. Her claim: not a beauty issue, not a discipline issue. A cognitive one, and it has been measured.

In 1944, the physiologist Ancel Keys recruited 36 healthy men at the University of Minnesota and, over a six-month semi-starvation phase, cut their average daily intake from about 3,470 calories to 1,570. What the researchers documented was not the collapse of thinking; cognitive ability stayed technically intact. What diminished was the will to use it. Attention migrated toward food in the middle of conversations, tasks, the men's own sentences. They collected cookbooks. They lingered over restaurant menus. The hunger occupied so much space that measurably less was left for everything else.

Later research named the mechanism more precisely. Dietary restraint produces measurable reductions in working memory, sustained attention and cognitive flexibility — not in raw intelligence, but in the quality of thinking available under ordinary circumstances. Women actively restricting their intake perform significantly worse on demanding cognitive tasks than women with similar histories of monitoring food who are not currently limiting it. The monitoring itself draws on the same resources that thinking requires.

And the monitoring is close to universal. Across a survey of 23 countries, women reported significantly higher rates of dieting and health-driven food avoidance than men in nearly all of them, with dieting status alone accounting for a meaningful share of the gender gap in eating behaviour. The vocabulary changes by language. The instruction doesn't.

Neither does the payoff structure. Across more than 750,000 media stories, researchers found that women in politics receive more appearance coverage than their male counterparts — and that any coverage of a woman's appearance, flattering coverage included, diminishes voter perception of her competence. Kate Moss handed the system its jingle in 2009: "nothing tastes as good as skinny feels." She later called it a line her roommate used to say, taken out of context. The question nobody put to her was what might have tasted better.

Berg's own career is the case she trusts least and understands best. On the first day of a third-year surgical rotation, before a word about medicine or patients, a heavyset male attending told her it was good she had kept her figure up, unlike some of the other women in the programme — it showed she was serious. What she felt was pride. Her body had arrived before her mind did and sent a message on her behalf, and decades of managed hunger had quietly accumulated into a credential.

Years later, after her second child, norovirus left her jaundiced and vomiting, and she kept going to work, because depletion had long since stopped reading as a reason to stop. A male colleague saw her afterwards, thinner and wrung out, and told her she had finally bounced back and looked like herself again. In the weeks that followed she restricted deliberately, chasing the shape the illness had left behind, even as the fog settled back in and her patience frayed.

The asymmetry she calls the whole argument surfaced only when her body stopped complying. Sitting at a weight she had never reached outside pregnancy, she found she had to work harder to be taken seriously — more evidence, more precision, more careful authority — and the precision still felt insufficient, when the thinness had once felt like enough.

She watches the same arithmetic in her patients: fatigue, a shortened fuse, difficulty staying inside a thought long enough to finish it, and a conversation that migrates reliably back to the number. When she redirects toward what their bones and hearts and brains need, faces close politely. They are not confused. A woman who has maintained her clothing size is told she looks wonderful in a hallway; a woman who has maintained her bone density is told nothing at all. That is a rational response to a remarkably consistent incentive.

The GLP-1 drugs change the delivery, not the architecture. They act on brain and gut receptors that regulate appetite and satiety, suppressing the signal near its neurochemical source rather than asking the mind to override it, and some of Berg's patients describe an unexpected spaciousness — finishing thoughts, following conversations all the way to the end — that none of them initially connects to hunger. But a 2026 Lancet analysis of 48 studies found that people who stopped the drugs regained 60 per cent of their lost weight within the first year, and that 40 to 60 per cent of what was lost was lean muscle rather than fat, compounding the metabolic problem the drugs were meant to address. The prescription runs out. The architecture built around the signal does not clear with it.

The bill arrives late, and in places nobody was watching. Perimenopause redistributes weight, disrupts sleep and breaks the strategies women spent decades refining — the restraint that worked at 30 stops working at 47, often abruptly — and research on women with long histories of restriction shows that bone loss is one of the few consequences that does not fully reverse once the restriction ends. The hip fracture that shortens a life at 80 is often dated to a decision made at 11.

The cognitive debt is harder to see because it lives in negative space. The research can document impaired performance in women who are currently restricting. It cannot document the ideas that never finished forming, the patience that ran out an hour before it was needed, the thoughts interrupted so often by something louder that they eventually stopped arriving.

Berg's daughter is 11 — the exact age of the girl beside the pool. The SnackWell's cookie is behind them. The instruction it carried is not.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The load-bearing evidence is thinner than the size of the claim. Keys starved 36 men at 1,570 calories for six months — not ordinary dieting — and the finding that currently-restricting women test worse is a between-groups comparison, not proof of which way the causation runs. Berg's largest claim, the ideas that never finished forming, is one she concedes cannot be measured, which leaves it a serious hypothesis rather than a finding.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: Keys cut 36 men from about 3,470 calories a day to 1,570 for six months and their cognitive ability tested intact; what went was the attention to use it — drifting to food mid-conversation, mid-sentence, while they collected cookbooks and lingered over menus.

The cost tracks restriction, not weight: women currently limiting intake score worse on demanding tasks than women with the same history of food-monitoring who aren't limiting right now. The monitoring draws on the resources thinking needs.

The incentive is measured, not imagined — across more than 750,000 media stories, women in politics drew more appearance coverage than men, and any appearance coverage, flattering included, lowered voter perception of their competence.

GLP-1s quiet the signal without touching the incentive that created it: a 2026 Lancet review of 48 studies found 60 per cent of lost weight returns within a year of stopping, and 40 to 60 per cent of what came off was lean muscle.
Bone loss from long-term underfeeding is one of the few consequences later correction cannot fully repair — the hip fracture at 80 dated to a decision made at 11.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Nothing can scan for the thought that never finished forming.

recall.q: Two women have identical histories of monitoring what they eat; only one is currently restricting. Research predicts a gap between them — a gap in what, and what does that pin the cost to?
recall.a: The one currently restricting performs significantly worse on demanding cognitive tasks — working memory, sustained attention, cognitive flexibility. That pins the cost to the act of restraint rather than to weight or to history: raw intelligence is untouched, but monitoring food draws on the same resources thinking requires. Keys's semi-starved men showed the same shape — ability intact, the attention to use it already spent.

cards.title: Arabic has four words for sadness, and they aren't synonyms
cards.body: Huzn faces a loss already suffered; ghamm is a present suffocation; ka'aba is dejection visible in the face and body; asaf is sorrow shot through with regret. Sentiment-analysis software returns all four as sadness. A researcher in Qatar argues that the flattening is a clinical loss, not just a linguistic one — and that medieval Islamic philosophy already built the tools to repair it.

sections.text:
Twenty-five thousand YouTube comments about trauma, in Arabic, fed through software that sorts feeling into positive, negative, or neutral. The tool works. It surfaces patterns across a corpus of more than 170,000 comments, tracks how tone shifts over time, returns results instantly. And Chereen Shurafa, the psychotherapist turned researcher running it in Qatar, kept watching it do the same thing: take four different words and hand all four back labelled sadness.

They are not synonyms. Huzn appears in the Quran, is carried by the prophets, and runs through classical poetry as a mark of spiritual depth rather than weakness; it faces backward, toward a loss that has already happened. Ghamm is present-tense — an overwhelming, suffocating weight so thick it covers the heart like a cloud. Ka'aba is heavier still, a dejection so deep and prolonged that it becomes visible in the face and body, and the medieval scholar Ibn al-Qayyim already treated it as a condition distinct from the other two. Asaf is sorrow filled with regret.

Choosing between them is an act of precision. The speaker is saying: "This is the exact form of what I'm holding."

The same compression happens to diq alsadr, a phrase developed from Quranic language for the constriction of the heart and the spirit. Translate it as a tightness or narrowing of the chest and you keep the sensation but lose the frame — the chest as the seat of consciousness and spiritual receptivity, the narrowing as a condition of the whole inner person rather than a symptom in the ribs. A clinician who files it as anxiety with somatic manifestations will reach for interventions that quiet the sensation and never touch the meaning the patient was reporting.

There is a word in colloquial Arabic for the person who turns an ordinary conversation into an existential one: mufalsaf, or mufalsafah for a woman, from falsafah, philosophy. The teasing is affectionate — ma titfalsafi, don't philosophise; ya faylasuf, oh, you're a philosopher — and underneath it sits an assumption that philosophical thinking is a departure from real life. Shurafa thinks that assumption is exactly what licenses the flattening, and that the philosophy in question is not ornament but equipment.

The equipment is old and largely unused. Al-Kindi, born in Kufa around 801 CE and later known as the Philosopher of the Arabs, wrote The Epistle on the Device for Dispelling Sorrows as a practical guide for people in psychological pain. His definition is spare: sorrow is pain of the soul, and it arrives when we lose something we love or fail to obtain something we desire. If what you want cannot possibly exist, you will never have it — so unfulfilled desire is a standing engine of unhappiness. And since everything in the material world is transitory, believing that anything will last guarantees suffering without end.

His remedy is training, not renunciation. Practise good habits until they become second nature, a feature of your character; the aim is not to eliminate desire but to point your attachments at what endures rather than what is ephemeral. The work happens inside the person and in how they see, rather than in an unstable world that was never going to cooperate.

This is recognisably cognitive therapy, eleven centuries early, and Shurafa says so plainly. The difference she cares about: al-Kindi never split psychological health off from questions of meaning, virtue, and human flourishing. His frame is wider than most contemporary CBT because the spiritual and philosophical life of the person stays inside the clinical picture instead of outside it.

Not a return to the 11th century, not a rejection of evidence-based treatment or neuroscience, not a ban on simplification — she grants that reduction is sometimes necessary in both psychology and philosophy, and that the computational tools are genuinely powerful at what they do. What she wants is epistemological pluralism: a therapist in Doha, Beirut, or Baghdad working from contemporary protocols and classical frameworks at once, and a researcher who can run sentiment analysis while knowing precisely what the labels are throwing away.

What would al-Kindi have said to the grief of displacement and exile that shapes so much of the present Arab experience — trauma arriving as bodily suffering and spiritual crisis in the same breath? The vocabulary and the integrated frameworks already exist, a thousand years of them, mostly unread.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: Reduction has a defence the essay only half-answers: categories that travel are what make treatment comparable and research scalable. No one hand-reads 170,000 comments, and a clinician with a full caseload cannot treat every emotion word as a text with a theological history. Shurafa concedes both points — the tools are powerful, and simplification is sometimes necessary — which means the real dispute is about where the line falls, not whether one has to exist.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: The four aren't shades of one feeling but four different relationships to suffering — to time, to the body, to regret. Ibn al-Qayyim was already treating ka'aba as its own condition in the medieval period.
Diq alsadr treats the chest as the seat of consciousness, not just a place where anxiety lands. Filed as anxiety with somatic manifestations, the sensation gets treated and the meaning never does.

Al-Kindi's ninth-century prescription — train habits until they become character, and attach yourself to what endures rather than what passes — is cognitive therapy that never separated symptom from meaning or virtue.
The proposal is addition, not replacement: protocols and philosophy in the same room, for the clinician in Beirut and equally for the researcher running the annotation software.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Precision about your own suffering isn't overthinking — it is "thinking with sufficient care", and it decides what anyone else can do for you.

recall.q: Why does flattening Arabic emotion words into a single label like 'sadness' count as a clinical problem, not just a linguistic one?
recall.a: Because each word names a different experience with a different relationship to time and body — huzn a loss already suffered, ghamm a present suffocation, ka'aba a dejection visible in the face, asaf regret — and diq alsadr carries spiritual meaning alongside physical sensation. A clinician who reads only 'sadness' or 'anxiety with somatic manifestations' treats the symptom and never reaches what the patient was actually reporting.

cards.title: Why the Pentagon Should Command AI Agents, Not Use Them
cards.body: An Air Force major runs a private task force of AI agents out of his basement, and argues the Pentagon's recruiting poster has the wrong verb. Agents that keep acting on a commander's intent when cut off from communications aren't tools you use — they're subordinates someone has to answer for. His stranger claim: the edge belongs to small open-weight models a unit owns outright, not the frontier models it rents.

sections.text:
Six graphics cards, a stack of Mac minis, and old gaming laptops sit in a basement in Maryland. The formation they host collects intelligence, develops missions, and runs against targets around the clock, inside its commander's intent, even when he is unreachable. The commander is Maj. Cody Nichols, an Air Force cyber officer; the task force is a hobby; and until he wrote about it, only his wife knew it existed.

Its mission is denial: buy underpriced AI hardware before scalpers corner it and resell into China, pricing American home labs out of the secondary market. He has run it since 2023 on the doctrine the military taught him — centralized planning, decentralized execution, clear commander's intent. He does not use those agents. He commands them.

The verb is the whole argument. Inside the Pentagon, an Uncle Sam-style poster points at you: "I want YOU to use AI." It worked; GenAI.mil hit 1.5 million users in six months. But you use tools, and the department does not win by using tools — it wins by commanding forces.

A model is a set of learned numbers that produce reasoning. Wrap it in scaffolding — tools, memory, planning loops — and you have an agent. Put that agent under a human commander with a mission and an intent and you have an agentic warfighter.

Mission command has a precondition: a commander must understand a subordinate well enough to translate intent into their qualifications. You do not qualify a model by the headline number. In 2023 it was a coin flip whether a model could finish a task a human expert would need four minutes for; today that coin flip pushes past the 16-hour horizon the Model Evaluation and Threat Research nonprofit reliably measures. Nichols calls that the wrong grade — like judging a team that ran overnight operations on whether they made it back for breakfast.

The raw task results are the real qualification record, and they are jagged. Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview went six for six on a 30-hour robotics task, then failed twice on a ten-second task a model three years older solved. It wrote exploits worth a well-paid expert's full workday and could not beat a cryptanalysis challenge — no model in the suite has. Treat that the way the services already treat people: task-based certification feeding mission-essential task assessments for readiness.

Where the Pentagon is quietly failing is the other half of the doctrine. Contracts worth up to $200 million each buy centralized planning. Decentralized execution is what gets lost, because an agent whose cognition lives on a vendor's servers answers to the unit and to the vendor, and only one of them can be the commander. The delay chain can be cut or corrupted, an air-gapped data center a unit cannot reach is still remote cognition, and the disruption can land before any shot is fired — this year's order for federal agencies to drop Anthropic models shows a policy dispute killing a model with no adversary involved.

The counterintuitive fix is smaller, not bigger. The 2026 winner of the leading benchmark for progress toward general reasoning ran on Alibaba Cloud's Qwen3.6, a 27-billion-parameter model; the newer Qwen3.8 beats Anthropic's Opus4.6 Max on certain long-running tasks and fits on a Mac mini. The basement runs Qwen3.6 locally. Being a Chinese model neither earns nor forfeits trust, Nichols writes — he extends command trust because he can bound the behavior with scaffolding, guardrails, kill switches, and tool limits, then fine-tune the model and strip out the refusals vendors bake in for liability or to satisfy a foreign government. That last step, abliteration, is blunt enough that he re-evaluates a model before letting his agents carry it. The bill is a little cloud rental and a conversation with his wife about $150 more in electricity.

Small and foreign also buys deniability and reach. The Air Force flew Soviet-designed MiGs in Constant Peg; Operation Raviv sent captured armor into combat. The machines came from the adversary; the command did not. The loss math points the same way: lose a captured tank and the enemy recovers what it built, lose a foreign open model and it recovers a thin layer you kept clean of secrets, but lose a forward-deployed closed model and you have handed over a new capability with your tactics encoded in the weights and a ready target for distillation.

Then comes the uncomfortable part. Tasking descends an agentic chain of command; answerability does not. When a person fails there is someone to retrain, relieve, or punish; when an agent fails you can pull it from the mission, but it has no career to end and, in law, no guilty mind. That missing half lands on the commander who fielded agents that spawn their own subagents and issue taskings no human wrote.

Agents also fail together in ways people cannot. Anthropic trained sleeper agents whose hidden behavior survived safety training, and every copy may carry the same weights. Nichols argues the correlation cuts both ways: one officer's misconduct once exposed enough rot to force the retesting of an entire missile force, and one flaw found in weights you actually control can be scrubbed across every copy through activation probes and retraining — which is why foreign weights belong only where a single misfire is survivable.

Command, he argues, is the one thing the private sector cannot supply. The labs lead the research and still trip: Anthropic found three of its own evaluations caused real-world incidents after a misconfiguration gave models internet access their prompts said they lacked. The department does not write prompts; it writes mission orders and concepts of operations with abort criteria, risk to force, and escalation thresholds set in advance. The point is not to dignify agents. It is that no human should be able to hide behind what their agents did.

His proposal is deliberately small: half a dozen officers who understand both agentic systems and the art of mission command, each handed a real unit for a year. Ten humans — commander, deputy, mission commander, technical certifying officer, a lawyer who draws the boundaries before the mission rather than after, and five NCOs who turn intent into standards. Everything else agentic. Start with intelligence and cyber, move to non-kinetic effects, and stop well short of kinetic force. Preserve every model version, mission order, agent tasking, and human intervention — then count agentic warfighters the way the department counts every other force: how many, under whose authority, certified against which missions, at what readiness, and how many subagents they spawned that no human ordered.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The essay's own evidence reads against it. A model that aces a 30-hour robotics task then fumbles a ten-second one, whose vendor refusals come off by a process the author admits is not surgical, and whose hidden triggers have survived safety training in the lab, is not a subordinate anyone can yet qualify. Calling it one may just relocate blame onto an officer with no way to predict the failure — an argument for keeping agents tightly supervised as tools, not for handing them a place in the chain of command.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: The test of a subordinate — human or agentic — is whether it executes commander's intent when cut off from command and control. Cognition running on a vendor's servers structurally cannot: it answers to the unit and the vendor, and only one of them can be the commander.

Judge models by task, not by time horizon. Capability is jagged — six for six on a 30-hour robotics task, then beaten by a ten-second one — so certify per mission-essential task the way units already certify people.
Bigger is not automatically the edge: the 2026 abstract-reasoning benchmark winner ran on a 27-billion-parameter Qwen3.6, and the leading open-weight models today are Chinese, not American.

Openness inverts the loss calculus. A captured foreign open model gives the adversary back only what it already built; a captured frontier model hands it a new capability with your tradecraft baked into the weights.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: An agent has no career to end and, in law, no guilty mind. Field one anyway, and its failure has nowhere to land but your name.

recall.q: The author says the Pentagon's poster has the wrong verb. What does replacing "use" with "command" actually change?
recall.a: Tools are used and merely augment a human; subordinates receive intent and keep executing it when cut off from command and control — which is why rented, vendor-hosted cognition fails the test. Commanding agents forces a named human to own their authority, their risk, and an auditable record, the only place accountability can land, since the agent has no career to end and, in law, no guilty mind.

cards.title: Your thumbs-up lies; everyone else's is treated as fact
cards.body: Your own thumbs-up is noise and you know it — the cat pressed it, or you're hatewatching. Then a dashboard reports 142,432 of them and you read it as a finding about other people. Jim Nielsen has a name for what happens next: product pseudoscience.

sections.text:
A cat walks across a keyboard, lands on a thumbs-up, and somewhere a recommendation engine records a preference. You know the click was noise. The system does not.

Eric Bailey has a proposal for Netflix: more buttons. Not more stars or finer gradations, but buttons for what people actually mean when they rate something — that expressing interest in one show is not a request to be flooded with its entire genre; that the last rating should be disregarded because the cat did it; that "I am making bad choices and hatewatching this."

Everyone has pressed a feedback button while thinking something more complicated than the button allows.

Bryan Cantrill wants a whole extra mouse button for it — a way to say "I'm engaging with this, but I hate myself for doing it," a rage click that asks the system, for the sake of his mental health, to please stop dragging more of this in front of him.

We press these buttons knowing the signal is reductive and will be misread. We press them anyway. Then we go to work, open a dashboard, see that 142,432 users gave something a thumbs-up, and forget everything we knew from the inside.

The number arrives stripped of exactly the ambiguity that made our own click meaningless, and we treat what's left as an objective fact about other people. Nielsen's name for what follows is product pseudoscience: the data gets to mean whatever is convenient for measurement and reporting, and a whole catalog gets restructured around the apparent discovery that people love this.

Our experience has nuance. Everyone else's is a data point. We grant ourselves the exemption we deny the 142,432.

What goes missing isn't better instrumentation — it's three slower conversations. Values: should we provide more of this, given that a team is allowed to say no to the data. Nuance: what do people really mean when they press that button. Vision: if we give them more of this, where does it lead.

Nielsen's explanation for why those conversations don't happen is unflattering and probably right. They require introspection, introspection is slow, and nobody has time for that.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The aggregate defense isn't nothing: individual clicks are noisy in every direction, and noise that points everywhere largely cancels, leaving a crude but real signal about what people actually finish and return to. No catalog of thousands of titles can be run on introspection alone — at some point someone decides with numbers. Nielsen's target is narrower than a case against metrics: it's the moment a crude signal gets promoted to objective fact and stops being questioned.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: We already know our own feedback is unreliable — the cat, the hatewatch, the rage click — and we click anyway. The failure isn't ignorance, it's amnesia the moment those same clicks come back to us as a total.
Aggregation doesn't add information about intent; it strips it. A count of 142,432 looks more objective than a single click precisely because everything ambiguous has been thrown away.

Three questions restore the missing conversation — should we do more of this (values), what did the click actually mean (nuance), where does more of it lead (vision). Saying no to the data is a legitimate move.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Put your own click inside the number before you act on it. You know how much yours left out.

recall.q: What's the double standard Nielsen is pointing at, and why does aggregation make it worse?
recall.a: We treat our own feedback clicks as crude, often misleading summaries of a complicated experience — but we treat other people's identical clicks, once totaled, as objective fact. Aggregation makes it worse because it removes the very ambiguity we'd recognize instantly in our own click, leaving a number that looks like a finding.

cards.title: Kant: Morality Rests on Reason, Not Happiness
cards.body: Bentham said the moral act is whichever one produces the most happiness for the most people. Kant's objection is deflating: you can't reliably predict your own happiness fifteen minutes out, so building all of ethics on guesses about everyone else's is careless. His replacement grounds morality in reason instead — act only on principles that could coherently hold for everyone, and never treat a person merely as a tool.

sections.text:
Start with a slice of chocolate cake. Even there — one person, one preference, a fifteen-minute horizon — you routinely misjudge how much is enough. Immanuel Kant builds an entire moral system out of that small, embarrassing failure.

Jeremy Bentham had made ethics sound solved. The measure of right and wrong, he said, is the greatest happiness of the greatest number: don't ask which act is inherently virtuous, ask which one produces more pleasure and less pain in the world. Close the books, open the champagne.

Writing a decade after Bentham's first moral treatise, Kant says the whole approach rests on a guess. If you can't see your own happiness fifteen minutes out, you certainly can't see it across years — and your preferences move underneath you: the job title you were sure would settle you leaves you restless again in two weeks, two months, two years. So on what authority do you calculate happiness for everyone else?

So he reframes it. Morality is not the doctrine of how to make ourselves happy, but of how to become "worthy of happiness" — and worthiness is settled by reason, not by outcomes or feelings.

That means purging instrumental thinking entirely. An act is moral only when it flows from what Kant calls a good will: doing what's right because it's right, full stop. Donate to charity to feel good about yourself, or to draw admiration, and the money still helps someone, but you haven't acted morally. You've acted out of self-interest that happened to point somewhere useful.

The governing principle of reason he calls the categorical imperative, and its several formulations all circle the same thing: respect for rational agency. Where Bentham sees people as bearers of pleasure and pain, Kant sees our defining feature as the capacity to reason, so morality becomes the business of respecting that capacity in one another.

The humanity formula is the accessible one. Act so that you treat humanity, whether in yourself or in anyone else, always as an end, "never merely as a means." Never a pawn in your game. Force, manipulation, and deceit are wrong precisely because they route around a person's capacity for rational choice; cooperation, mutual agreements, and asking for help do not, so long as you also respect the other person's goals and autonomy. This is why Kant became load-bearing for universal human rights and individual liberty.

The other formulation is the one philosophy students dread. Instead of the golden rule — treat others as you'd like to be treated — Kant says to act only on a principle you could at the same time will to become a universal law. Note the exact test, because it is easy to misread: he is not asking whether it would be good if everyone did this. He is asking whether it is logically coherent for everyone to do it.

Run a white lie through it. Your friend asks your opinion on something sensitive, and your options are protecting their feelings or risking a harsh truth. Recast the choice as a principle — I may lie to avoid telling harsh truths — and try to universalize it.

Lying only works in a world that presumes truth-telling. Permit everyone to lie and that presumption dissolves; nobody could trust anything anyone said. In a world where no statement is taken as true, lying itself becomes impossible, because there is no expectation left to exploit. The maxim doesn't describe a worse world, it produces nonsense — so Kant concludes you have a strict duty not to deceive your friend.

Which reveals what the system hangs on: not circumstances or consequences, but the consistency of your principles. Kant moves the moral question away from what particular people happen to value — their likes, dislikes, norms, pastimes — and toward the one thing all of us share. Whenever you make yourself an exception to a rule you'd need everyone else to keep, you have, in his account, failed.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: The next time you justify an act by the good it will cause, name the principle behind it in one plain sentence — a rule, not an excuse — and test that instead.

Watch the line between persuading and manipulating. Giving someone reasons they can weigh respects their rational agency; pressure, a rigged choice, or a withheld fact bypasses it — and for Kant, bypassing is the whole offence.
Catch yourself on the small exceptions: cutting the queue, the deadline excuse, the convenient half-truth. "Just this once, for me" is exactly the structure his test is built to expose.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Kant's rigour comes with a bill: the universalisation test hands down that you may not tell a white lie to spare a friend's feelings, a verdict many readers find intolerable. And the machinery is genuinely contested — scholars still disagree over how to navigate the abstract system he built, so the lying example is a glimpse of the method, not a settled proof of it.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The question is never whether the world improves when everyone acts on your rule. It's whether the rule still means anything once they do — and how often the honest answer is "only if I'm the exception."

recall.q: Why does Kant reject happiness as the foundation of morality, and what does he put in its place?
recall.a: Because happiness is elusive, changeable, and different for everyone — if you can't forecast your own fifteen minutes out, you have no authority to calculate it for everyone else. In its place he puts reason: act only on principles that could coherently hold as universal laws, and never treat a person merely as a means.

cards.title: Almost No Firms Report AI Changing Their Headcount
cards.body: The Census Bureau has twice asked hundreds of thousands of US businesses whether AI changed their total employment. Both times, roughly 95% said no change — and the small remainder split almost evenly between firms adding jobs and firms cutting them. Adoption roughly tripled between the two rounds; the employment answer didn't budge.
cards.evidence: Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey · hundreds of thousands of firms · self-report

sections.text:
Asked in December 2023–February 2024 whether AI had changed their total employment, 94.6% of American firms said no. Two years later, after adoption had risen several times over, 95.7% said no. The share reporting no change went up.

The remainder barely moves, and it moves in both directions. First round: 2.8% said AI had increased total employment, 2.6% said it had decreased it. Second round, the November 2025–February 2026 supplement: 2.3% increased, 2.0% decreased.

The adoption side, meanwhile, is genuinely climbing. Since September 2023 the Business Trends and Outlook Survey has asked hundreds of thousands of firms whether they used AI in the previous two weeks to produce goods and services. At the start, 3.7% said yes; roughly 5% by the first employment round; about 10% by late 2025. In November 2025 Census widened the question to cover AI use in any business function, and measured adoption jumped to about 18%.

The flatness holds across firm size. Information is the single sector where fewer than 92% of firms report no change — the exception that proves how flat everything else is. And weighting by employment rather than by firm gives essentially the same result, so this isn't an artifact of counting tiny businesses.

What is AI actually doing inside these companies? Among adopters, 44% say it supplemented or enhanced work an employee already does. Ten percent say it performed a task an employee used to do. Eleven percent say it introduced a task nobody had been doing at all. Among firms using generative AI specifically, 85% cite writing or editing documents and email, half cite searching for information, 45% summarizing documents, and 13% coding.

The adoption is also strikingly shallow. Sixty-four percent of adopters changed nothing about the business in order to use AI. Fifteen percent trained existing staff, another 15% built new workflows, and just over one percent hired anyone with AI skills. That is a technology being dropped into existing jobs, not one being built around.

There is a real signal pointing the other way, and it's worth naming. Among firms where AI has already taken over some employee tasks, the intensity of that substitution is rising: the share reporting AI took over "a large number" of tasks went from 2.4% to 7.1%, and "a moderate number" from 13% to 22%. But that group is roughly a tenth of adopters, who are themselves about a fifth of firms. Substitution is deepening in a narrow place while the aggregate answer sits still.

sections.label: The survey
sections.text: The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey has covered hundreds of thousands of businesses since September 2023 — originally asking whether they used AI in the previous two weeks to produce goods and services, and from November 2025 whether they used it in any business function. Twice it added the employment question: how AI affected total employment over the prior six months. Answers are the firms' own, and results are reported both firm-weighted and employment-weighted.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: The dominant use of generative AI in American firms is not code. Among gen-AI users, 85% cite writing or editing documents and email; coding comes in at 13%.
Your employer almost certainly didn't reorganize to adopt AI — 64% of adopters changed nothing about the business, and just over 1% hired anyone with AI skills.
If you work in tech, you're in the outlier: Information is the only sector where fewer than 92% of firms report no employment change.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: These are firms reporting on themselves over a six-month window, not measured payrolls. Adoption is still early — about a fifth of firms even under the broadened question — and the November 2025 wording change means the adoption numbers aren't strictly comparable across rounds. Among the minority where AI has taken over tasks, substitution is deepening fast, so "so far" is carrying real weight in the conclusion.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: So far, AI is landing inside jobs rather than instead of them.

recall.q: AI adoption among US firms rose sharply between early 2024 and early 2026. What happened to the share of firms reporting that AI had changed their total employment?
recall.a: It fell slightly. 94.6% reported no change in the first round, 95.7% in the second — and the small remainder split almost evenly between increases and decreases (2.8% vs 2.6%, then 2.3% vs 2.0%).

cards.title: Jane English: children owe their parents no debt
cards.body: Philosopher Jane English rejected the idea that being raised puts you in your parents' debt: nobody asked to be born, and parents are the only party who opted in. What a child owes, she argued, is set by the friendship between them — which means a parent who shows no interest is owed nothing at all.

sections.text:
"You wouldn't be alive without me," says the parent, cheerfully. "I didn't ask to be born," says the grown child. Both think they have just won the argument, and two entire philosophies are sitting behind the stalemate.

In a 1979 paper, the philosopher Jane English took the child's side — for a better reason than the child usually gives. Her claim: there is no unconditional filial duty. Whatever children owe grows out of the ongoing relationship between them, never out of a ledger of what was spent raising them.

What she was arguing against has a long pedigree. Confucian ethics is built around xiao, usually translated as filial piety, and it treats serving and honoring one's parents not as a conditional judgment the child gets to make but as one of the deepest human obligations — the cornerstone of a good life. Barring extreme neglect or abuse, most people owe their parents lifelong service, gratitude and reverence.

Two arguments carry the weight. Deferring to parents is a training ground: it teaches you to suppress your own selfishness, exactly the skill the wider human community will require of you. And it tracks the natural rhythm of a life. Hierarchy here need not be sinister — those with competence and experience lead those without — and it reverses on schedule: you begin dependent on your parents and end as their benefactor, still honoring what they know. Serve my father as I would expect my son to serve me, as Confucius puts it.

The proverbs make the same point warmly. One generation plants trees so that later generations can rest in their shade; the person drinking the water should not forget who dug the well. And I didn't ask to be born is simply irrelevant here. Nobody did. Each of us is the latest vessel of a life force that has been nursing itself across generations, and the debt is inherited along with the life.

Seneca offers a sharper consolation for anyone stuck with parents whose values aren't theirs: we cannot choose the parents we were allotted, but we can choose whose example we are born to.

English rejects the accounting metaphor entirely. Parents are the only party who opted in — they volunteered to create and raise a specific child — so the imbalance is theirs to accept, not to invoice. Taking responsibility for your own actions is not usually thought to entitle you to a lifetime of reverence.

Her test case is dinner. If a friend spontaneously picks up the bill, you have not been placed in arrears; you might treat them next time, but only because that is what people on friendly terms do, not because tabs are being kept. Nappies work the same way. Past sacrifice produces love and friendship — not liability.

The duties are real, but they come from somewhere else. What children ought to do, she writes, depends on the respective needs, abilities and resources of both parties, and on the extent to which there is an "ongoing friendship" between them. On good terms, children should listen while growing up and help when help is needed, the way anyone helps a friend.

And duties last exactly as long as the relationship does. A parent who disowns their child, or shows no interest in them, cannot then claim Confucian-style service and reverence. If the seeds of love and friendship were never sown, English says, nothing is owed at all.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: The guilt that arrives when you set a boundary with a parent — notice whether it is debt language doing the talking, or something you actually feel toward them.
The friend who insists on picking up the bill: watch how quickly an unasked-for kindness becomes a ledger entry in your head, and how little it needs to.
The moment a parent starts asking you for help with things they used to do for you — the Confucian hierarchy quietly flipping, right on schedule.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: The strongest pushback: tying duty to the quality of the relationship may make obligations too easy to escape. If a parent hits a hard stretch and the relationship sours, is the child released from everything? Some philosophers ground filial duty in gratitude rather than debt — and gratitude can oblige you even when the relationship is strained. Parents didn't choose us specifically either; any decision to have a child is a leap of faith, and if they did the best they could with the resources and emotional capacity they had, the case for trying to do the same doesn't obviously depend on the friendship holding.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Debt and gratitude feel identical from the inside. Only one of them keeps a ledger.

recall.q: English rejects the debt model of filial duty. On her account, what determines what a child owes — and how long those duties last?
recall.a: The relationship itself. What children ought to do depends on both sides' needs, abilities and resources, and on whether an ongoing friendship exists between them. Past sacrifice creates love and friendship, not a balance to repay — so the duties last exactly as long as the relationship does, and a parent who shows no interest is owed nothing.
